cards.title: The Protégé Problem
cards.instruction: Treat another player as someone you trained. Offer corrections, backhanded praise, and reminders of your influence.

cards.title: Pick a Priority
cards.instruction: Make someone choose between two ordinary obligations that both supposedly cannot wait.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Use the priority list I taught you. Mum's at the station; her parcel's at the depot, which shuts at six. Which do I collect?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: It's her birthday present. Neither can wait.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Good, you've named both pressures. Now choose which disappointment you can explain to her.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Get the parcel. I'll phone her and explain.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: She's calling me already. Nearly a complete plan. Do I pull over to reassure her, or keep going for the present? You choose.

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 priority-list training frames collections; A3 grades B2 identifying pressure but requires choice; A5 calls B4 plan nearly complete and reopens choice at incoming-call delay.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 birthday relation causes A3 disappointment comparison; B4 parcel-first/call plan causes A5 current call versus driving conflict.

relationship.evidence: B4 reasonably takes on communication so A can collect, and the incoming call complicates that actual proposal.

heightening.evidence: A5 converts B4 chosen remedy into the next urgent tradeoff, keeping the pupil responsible for priority.

specificity.evidence: A1 station/depot/six and B4 call identify real tasks and deadline.
